surah.summary: A seven-verse prayer that opens the book and is said in every one of the daily prayers: praise of God as Lord of the worlds, Merciful, and Master of the Day of Judgment, then a plea to be guided on the straight path.

The longest surah, and the charter of the community at Medina. It sorts people into those who believe, those who refuse and those who only say they believe; retells Adam's fall and Israel's history as a warning; presents Abraham and Ishmael as the builders of the House at Mecca and turns the direction of prayer toward it; then gives law on food, retaliation, fasting, pilgrimage, fighting, marriage and divorce, charity, usury and debt. It holds the Throne Verse (255) and "no compulsion in religion" (256).

Named for the family into which Mary was born. It opens with the Book itself, some of whose verses are definitive and others open to more than one reading; tells of Mary, Zechariah, John and Jesus; and calls the People of the Book to a common word: to worship none but God. Its second half speaks to the believers after a defeat in battle (Uhud, by tradition): why it happened, who wavered, and that those killed in God's cause are alive with their Lord.

Law for the household and for a community at war. It sets out the care of orphans' property, marriage (up to four wives, if they can be treated fairly), the shares of inheritance, whom a man may not marry, and men's charge over women; commands obedience to God, the Messenger and those in authority; and deals with fighting, killing, emigration and the hypocrites who waver. It ends with the People of the Scripture: it denies that Jesus was killed or crucified, and tells them not to say "Three".

Among the last surahs, by tradition. It completes the law (food, hunting on pilgrimage, washing before prayer, oaths, wine and gambling forbidden, the penalties for theft and for making war on God and His Messenger) and says, "Today I have perfected your religion for you." Much of it is addressed to Jews and Christians: their broken pledges, judging by the Torah, the Gospel and this Book, and the denial that God is the Messiah or "the third of three". It ends with God questioning Jesus on the Last Day, and the table sent down from heaven.

A long Meccan argument against idolatry. It answers the Meccans' objections one by one (why no angel, no miracle, no book on paper), shows Abraham reasoning from the star, the moon and the sun to the one who made them, names eighteen prophets God guided, and sets aside the pagans' rules about which crops and animals are forbidden, giving in their place a short list of what God has forbidden (151 to 153).

Named for the Heights between the Garden and the Fire, where men stand who can see both. After Satan's refusal to bow to Adam and the loss of the Garden, it tells in one long sequence of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shuaib, each rejected by his people, who were then destroyed; and then, at greater length, of Moses: Pharaoh, the plagues, the sea, the calf and the mountain. It says the Unlettered Prophet is found in the Torah and the Gospel (157).

Tied by tradition to the first battle, Badr (the "Day of Distinction", verse 41). It settles who owns the spoils, explains the victory as God's doing, with angels sent to help, and gives rules of war: stand firm, do not flee, fight until persecution ends, keep treaties unless they are betrayed, prepare what force you can, and incline to peace if the enemy does. It ends with the bond between those who emigrated and those who sheltered them.

The only surah that does not open with "In the name of God", and among the last by tradition. It cancels the treaties of idolaters who broke them, orders that after the sacred months they be fought unless they repent (5), bars them from the Sacred Mosque, and orders fighting those of the People of the Scripture who do not follow the religion of truth until they pay the tax (29). Most of the rest concerns an expedition many did not want to join (Tabuk, by tradition): it exposes the hypocrites and their excuses, and praises those who strove.

A Meccan surah on revelation and those who deny it. They ask for a different Quran, or for a miracle, and are challenged to produce one chapter like it (38). Noah and Moses are recalled; Pharaoh believes as he drowns, too late. The surah is named for the one town that believed in time, the people of Jonah (98), and it asks the Prophet, "Will you compel people to become believers?" (99).

"Worship none but God", driven home by the stories of the messengers in order: Noah and the flood (and the son who would not board), Hud, Salih, the angels who visit Abraham on their way to Lot, Shuaib, and Moses. Each people refused and was destroyed. The stories are told, it says, to strengthen the Prophet's heart (120).

The one surah that tells a single story from beginning to end: Joseph's dream, the well, the wife of the Egyptian who bought him, prison, the king's dream, his charge over the storehouses of Egypt, and his reunion with his brothers and his father Jacob. In prison he preaches the one God (39 to 40). The surah calls the story a confirmation of what came before (111).

The signs of God in the sky and the earth (the thunder itself praises Him), set against those who ask for a miracle and doubt that dust can be raised. It says God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves (11), and that hearts find rest in the remembrance of God (28).

Messengers are sent in the language of their own people, to bring them out of darkness into light. The surah holds Satan's speech to those who followed him (22), the parable of a good word as a good tree (24 to 26), and Abraham's prayer for the barren valley by God's Sacred House, where he settled some of his offspring (35 to 41).

Named for al-Hijr, the Rock, whose people carved their homes in the mountains and were destroyed (80 to 84). God says He sent down the Message and will preserve it (9); Satan refuses to bow to a creature of clay; angels visit Abraham and then Lot. It ends by telling the Prophet to proclaim openly what he is commanded (94).

A catalogue of God's favors (cattle, rain, crops, the sea, the stars, milk, fruit, the bee and its honey) as signs that He alone is to be worshiped. It commands justice and kindness (90), speaks of one verse being put in place of another (101), excuses the one forced to deny his faith while his heart stays firm (106), and tells the Prophet to call to God's way with wisdom and good advice (125).

Opens with the journey by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (1). It gives a code of conduct (22 to 39): worship none but God, be good to parents, give to the poor, do not kill your children, do not come near adultery, do not kill unjustly, keep your pledge, give full measure. It challenges humans and jinn together to produce the like of the Quran (88), and says the Quran was revealed in stages (106).

Four stories: the young men who slept in a cave for three centuries; the owner of two gardens who forgot God; Moses and the servant of God, who did three things Moses could not bear to watch; and Dhul-Qarnayn, who traveled to the setting and the rising of the sun and built a barrier of iron against Gog and Magog.

Named for Mary. Zechariah is given John in his old age; Mary, alone, gives birth to Jesus beneath a palm tree, and the infant speaks from the cradle: "I am the servant of God." Then Abraham's break with his father, and Moses, Ishmael and Idris. Twice the surah rejects the saying that God has a son (35, 88 to 92).

Almost wholly the story of Moses, told more fully here than anywhere: the fire in the valley of Tuwa and the voice, "I am God; there is no god but I", the staff and the white hand, Aaron given as his helper, Pharaoh and the magicians, the sea, and the calf made at the prompting of "the Samiri" while Moses was away. It ends with Adam's forgetting in the Garden, and a call to patience and prayer.

The prophets in quick succession, each calling on God and being answered: Abraham, who breaks his people's idols and is saved from the fire; then Lot, Noah, David and Solomon, Job, Ishmael, Idris, Dhul-Kifl, Jonah, Zechariah, and Mary. All were told the same thing: "There is no god but I, so worship Me" (25). Of the Prophet it says, "We did not send you except as mercy to mankind" (107).

Meccan in its warnings and Medinan in its law. It begins with the terror of the Hour; gives the rites of pilgrimage to the House that Abraham was told to purify (26 to 37); and holds what tradition takes to be the first permission to fight, given "to those who are fought against", driven from their homes for saying "Our Lord is God" (39 to 40). The same verse names monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques as places where God's name is much mentioned.

Opens with a portrait of the believers who will inherit Paradise: humble in prayer, charitable, chaste, true to their trusts (1 to 11), and traces the making of a human being from clay to clot to flesh (12 to 14). Then come the messengers, each dismissed by his people as only a man, and the unbelievers' denial that the dead are raised.

Law for the household at Medina. It sets a hundred lashes for adultery and eighty for accusing a chaste woman without four witnesses (2 to 4); rebukes those who spread a slander (11 to 20: against the Prophet's wife Aisha, by tradition); tells men and women alike to restrain their looks, and women to draw their coverings over their breasts (30 to 31); and gives rules for entering homes. In its middle stands the Light Verse: "God is the Light of the heavens and the earth" (35).

Answers the Meccans' objections to the Prophet: that he is a man who eats food and walks in the markets, that the Quran is old tales dictated to him, that it did not come down all at once (32). It closes with a portrait of "the servants of the Merciful": humble, in prayer by night, moderate in spending, who neither kill nor commit adultery, and who repent (63 to 76).

Seven stories told to one refrain ("In that is a sign, but most of them are not believers. Your Lord is the Almighty, the Merciful"): Moses, Abraham, Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shuaib. Each messenger says the same words to his people: "Fear God, and obey me. I ask of you no payment." It ends by saying that the Quran was brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit in clear Arabic, not by devils, and that the Prophet is no poet.

Named for the ant that warned its fellows of Solomon's army. Its centerpiece is Solomon, who was taught the speech of birds, and the queen of Sheba, a worshiper of the sun, who comes to him and submits to God (15 to 44). A run of questions follows, each ending "Is there another god with God?" (60 to 64).

The early life of Moses: set adrift as an infant and taken in by Pharaoh's household, his killing of a man and flight to Midian, his marriage there, and the call at the fire. Pharaoh tells Haman to build him a tower to reach the God of Moses (38). Later comes Qarun (Korah), whose treasures the earth swallowed with him (76 to 82).

Asks whether people think they will be left to say "We believe" without being tested. Earlier peoples pass in review, and whoever takes a protector other than God is likened to the spider, whose house is the frailest of houses (41). It tells the believers to argue with the People of the Scripture only in the best manner, and to say, "Our God and your God is One" (46).

Begins with news: the Romans (the Byzantines) have been defeated in a nearby land, but within a few years will be victorious (2 to 4). The heart of the surah is a list of "His signs" (20 to 25): creation from dust, spouses with love and compassion between them, the variety of languages and colors, sleep, lightning and rain. It calls the worship of one God the nature on which God made mankind (30).

Named for Luqman, a man given wisdom, whose advice to his son it records (12 to 19): give God no partners, keep the prayer, urge what is right and forbid what is wrong, be patient, do not strut or shout. It commands gratitude to parents, but not obedience if they press their child to worship another besides God (14 to 15).

A short surah on revelation, creation and return. God made the heavens and the earth in six days and man from clay, breathing into him of His Spirit; the angel of death will take each soul; the guilty will beg to be sent back. Those who believe fall down in prostration when they are reminded of God's revelations (15), from which the surah has its name.

Named for the clans who besieged Medina (the battle of the Trench, by tradition; 9 to 27). Much of the rest concerns the Prophet's own household: adopted sons are not true sons, so he may marry the former wife of his adopted son Zayd (37); his wives are mothers to the believers, are to stay in their homes, and may never be married after him; and which women he may marry (50). It calls Muhammad "the seal of the prophets" (40), and lists the virtues of believing men and believing women side by side (35).

David, for whom iron was made soft, and Solomon, served by the wind and the jinn, whose death they did not notice until a worm ate through his staff (10 to 14); then the people of Sheba, whose gardens were ruined by the flood of the dam when they turned ungrateful (15 to 19). The rest argues with those who deny the Hour and trust in their wealth and numbers.

Praise of God as Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers with two, three and four wings. People are "the poor, in need of God" (15); no soul will carry another's burden (18); and those given the Book are of three kinds: those who wrong themselves, those who keep a middle course, and those foremost in good deeds (32).

It tells of a town that rejected three messengers and killed the one man who believed them (13 to 29), points to signs in the revived earth, the night, and the courses of the sun and the moon, and answers the one who asks "Who will revive the bones?": He who made them the first time (78 to 79). In Muslim tradition it is called the heart of the Quran, and is recited for the dying.

After the Day of Judgment, the Garden and the tree of Hell, it recalls the prophets, each with the refrain "Peace be upon him": Noah, Abraham, Moses and Aaron, Elijah, Lot and Jonah. Here Abraham sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son, who consents, and the son is ransomed "with a great sacrifice" (102 to 107). The son is not named; the good news of Isaac follows (112), and Muslim tradition mostly holds that the son was Ishmael.

Against the leaders of Mecca, who said, "Did he turn all the gods into one God?" (5), it sets David, tested by two disputants over a single ewe; Solomon, tested by his love of fine horses; and Job, patient under affliction. It ends with Satan's refusal to bow before the human being God made "with My own hands" (75).

Devotion to God alone: the idolaters say of their gods, "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God" (3). It holds one of the Quran's widest promises: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins" (53). It ends with the two throngs, one driven to the gates of Hell and one led to the gates of Paradise.

Opens by naming God "Forgiver of sins, Accepter of repentance, Severe in punishment" (3). Its centerpiece is a man of Pharaoh's own family who had hidden his faith and now speaks up for Moses: "Are you going to kill a man for saying, My Lord is God?" (28 to 45). It says God has told of some messengers and not of others (78), and that belief at the sight of the punishment comes too late (85).

A Quran "in Arabic for people who know", its verses set out in detail. It describes the making of the earth and the heavens over days, the end of Aad and Thamud, and the Day when people's own hearing, sight and skins will testify against them (20 to 22). Its counsel: "Repel evil with good, and the person who was your enemy becomes like an intimate friend" (34).

God has prescribed for the believers the same religion He enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus (13), and "there is nothing like Him" (11). The believers are those who "conduct their affairs by mutual consultation" (38), which gives the surah its name. A wrong may be repaid in kind, but to pardon is better (40). God speaks to a human only by inspiration, from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger (51).

Against the Meccans who call the angels daughters of God and follow the ways of their fathers. Wealth proves nothing: God could give the unbelievers roofs of silver and ornaments of gold, and it would be only the stuff of this life (33 to 35). Jesus is "a servant whom We blessed" and "a portent of the Hour" (59 to 61). "If the Most Gracious had a son, I would be the first to worship" (81).

The Book was sent down on "a Blessed Night" (3). The surah warns of a Day when the sky brings a visible smoke, recalls the army of Pharaoh, over whom "neither heaven nor earth wept" (29), and sets the tree that feeds the sinner in Hell against the gardens and springs of the righteous.

Signs in creation for those who reason, and a warning to whoever hears the verses and mocks. The deniers say, "There is nothing but this our present life; nothing destroys us except time" (24). On the Day, every community will be on its knees, each called to its record (28): hence the name of the surah.

The Prophet is told to say, "I am not different from the other messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me, or with you" (9). The surah commands kindness to parents, tells of Hud warning Aad among the sand dunes before the wind destroyed them, and of a company of jinn who listened to the Quran and went back to warn their people (29 to 32).

A Medinan surah on war, also called "Fighting". When the believers meet the unbelievers in battle they are to strike, then bind the captives, and afterward free them by grace or for ransom, "until war lays down its burdens" (4). It describes the Garden's rivers of water, milk, wine and honey (15), and rebukes those "in whose hearts is sickness", who look faint when fighting is commanded.

Tied by tradition to the truce of Hudaybiyya (628), which it calls "a conspicuous victory". God was pleased with the believers who pledged allegiance under the tree (18), held the two sides back from fighting "in the valley of Mecca" (24), and promises they will enter the Sacred Mosque in safety (27). It ends, "Muhammad is the Messenger of God", with a description of his followers said to be in the Torah and the Gospel (29).

Manners for the community: do not raise your voice above the Prophet's, check a report before acting on it, make peace between believers who fight, and do not mock, spy on or backbite one another. "We created you from a male and a female, and made you races and tribes, that you may know one another. The best among you in the sight of God is the most righteous" (13).

On death and rising. God is nearer to a person than his jugular vein, and two recorders sit at his right and his left (16 to 18). Then come the daze of death, the Trumpet, the driver and the witness. Hell is asked, "Are you full?" and answers, "Are there any more?" (30).

Oaths by the winds that the Judgment is true. Angels visit Abraham with news of a son and go on to the people of Lot; Pharaoh, Aad, Thamud and Noah's people each follow in a line or two. It gives the purpose of creation in a sentence: "I did not create the jinn and the humans except to worship Me" (56).

Swears by the Mount that the punishment is coming, and sets the Fire against the gardens of the righteous. The second half defends the Prophet against the names he was called (soothsayer, madman, poet) with a run of questions to his accusers: "Were they created out of nothing? Or are they the creators?" (35).

Defends what the Prophet saw: the one who taught him, on the highest horizon, and again by the Lotus Tree of the farthest limit (1 to 18). It names the three goddesses of Mecca, al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, and calls them nothing but names (19 to 23). Then it gives what was in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham: no soul bears another's burden, and a person has only what he strives for (36 to 41).

"The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split." Five peoples who rejected the warnings: Noah's, Aad, Thamud, Lot's and Pharaoh's, each followed by the refrain that the Quran has been made easy to remember, "Is there anyone who would remember?"

A hymn to God's favors, addressed to humans and jinn together, with one refrain asked thirty-one times: "So which of your Lord's marvels will you deny?" It moves from the creation (sun, moon, sea, pearls) to the passing of everything on earth, to Hell, and then to two pairs of gardens.

When "the Inevitable" comes, people will be sorted into three: the forerunners, brought nearest; those on the Right; and those on the Left (7 to 56). Four questions follow: is it you who create the seed, the crop, the rain, the fire, or We? (57 to 74). It calls the Quran a noble recitation in a well-protected Book (77 to 78).

God is "the First and the Last, the Outer and the Inner" (3). The believers are urged to give: those who gave and fought before the conquest rank above those who did so after it (10). This life is "play and distraction" (20). God sent down iron, with its violent force and its uses (25). Of those who followed Jesus it says God put compassion and mercy in their hearts, but that monasticism was their own invention (27).

Begins with a wife's complaint against her husband, who had put her away by the old formula of calling her as his mother to him: the formula is declared a lie, and a penalty is set for those who use it and then go back on it (1 to 4). It warns against secret counsels, and ends by saying that believers do not love those who oppose God and His Messenger, even their own kin (22).

Tells of "those who disbelieved among the People of the Book" driven from their fortresses and homes (the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir, by tradition), and how what was taken from them is to be shared among the Messenger, his relatives, the orphans, the poor and the emigrants. It closes with a list of the names of God: the Sovereign, the Holy, the Peace-Giver (22 to 24).

Believers are not to ally with those who drove them out. But "as for those who have not fought against you for your religion, nor expelled you from your homes, God does not prohibit you from dealing with them kindly and equitably" (8). Women who come as emigrants are to be tested in their faith and not sent back, and the terms of the women's pledge to the Prophet are given (12).

God loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, like a compact structure (4). Jesus announces "a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad" (6). The believers are offered a trade that will save them: faith, and striving with their possessions and their lives (10 to 11).

God sent a messenger to an unlettered people. Those entrusted with the Torah who did not uphold it are like a donkey carrying books (5). When the call to prayer is made on the day of congregation (Friday), the believers are to leave their business and hasten to it (9).

A portrait of the hypocrites of Medina: they bear witness with their tongues, use their oaths as a cover, and look impressive, "like propped-up timber" (4). It ends by urging the believers to give before death comes.

All things praise God, who made some people believers and some unbelievers. The Day of Gathering is the Day of "mutual exchange", of loss and gain (9). Wealth and children are a test, and there may be enemies even in one's own family; yet it urges pardon (14 to 15).

Rules of divorce: it is to be pronounced at the proper time and the waiting period counted (three months for those who do not menstruate, until delivery for the pregnant); the woman is not to be driven from her home, and she is to be housed and provided for. "Whoever fears God, He will make a way out for him" (2).

Addressed to the Prophet about a matter in his own household: he had forbidden himself something lawful to please his wives, and one wife had passed on a confidence. Two of them are told to repent (4). It ends with four women as examples: the wives of Noah and of Lot, who betrayed their husbands, and the wife of Pharaoh and Mary, who believed.

God created death and life to test which of you is best in conduct (2). The seven heavens show no flaw, however often one looks. The keepers of Hell ask each batch thrown in, "Has no warner come to you?" (8). It ends with questions: who provides for you, who holds up the birds, who would bring you water if yours drained away?

Among the earliest surahs. It assures the Prophet that he is not mad, and is of great moral character (2 to 4); tells of men who swore to harvest their garden at dawn, leaving nothing for the poor, and found it ruined (17 to 33); and bids him be patient, and not like "the fellow of the fish", Jonah (48).

"The Reality": Thamud, Aad and Pharaoh denied it and were destroyed. Then the Trumpet sounds once; each person is handed his book, in the right hand or in the left (19 to 37). It ends by swearing that this is the speech of a noble messenger, not of a poet or a soothsayer.

A questioner asks about the punishment to come, on a Day whose length is fifty thousand years. Man was created restless, fretful in hardship and grudging in good fortune, except those who pray, give the beggar his share, guard their chastity and keep their trusts (19 to 35).

Noah speaks throughout: he called his people night and day, in public and in private, and they put their fingers in their ears and clung to their gods Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Yauq and Nasr. He prays that no unbeliever be left on the earth.

A band of jinn overhear the Quran and believe: "We have heard a wondrous Quran. It guides to rectitude" (1 to 2). They report that heaven is now guarded against eavesdroppers. The Prophet is told to say he cannot harm or guide anyone, and does not know when the promise will come.

Among the first surahs: the Prophet, wrapped in his cloak, is told to stand in prayer for much of the night and recite the Quran, for "a heavy message" is coming (5). The last verse, which tradition dates later, eases the night vigil: "read of the Quran what is possible for you".

"Arise and warn" (2): by tradition, among the very first commands to preach. A wealthy man who weighed the Quran and called it magic and the word of a mortal is promised Saqar, the Fire, over which are nineteen keepers. The guilty are asked what brought them there: "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the destitute" (43 to 44).

"Does man think that We will not reassemble his bones?" (3). Faces on that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord, or gloomy. In the middle the Prophet is told not to hurry his tongue with the revelation: its gathering and its recitation are God's to see to (16 to 19).

Man was made from a drop, to be tested, and shown the way, whether he is grateful or not. The righteous "feed, for the love of Him, the poor, and the orphan, and the captive", wanting no thanks (8 to 9); their reward is described at length. The Quran was sent down gradually (23).
Oaths by "those sent forth" that what is promised will happen, with one refrain ten times over: "Woe on that Day to the deniers."

"What are they asking one another about? About the Great Event." The earth, the mountains, sleep, night and day, rain are recalled as signs; then the Day of Sorting, Hell lying in ambush, and gardens for the righteous. The denier will say, "I wish I were dust" (40).

Oaths by those who pull out souls; the Day of the Quake. Moses is sent to Pharaoh, who says, "I am your Lord, the most high" (24), and is seized. Is man harder to create than the sky? Whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained himself has Paradise for a home.

Opens with a rebuke: "He frowned and turned away when the blind man approached him", while giving his attention to one who felt no need (1 to 10): the Prophet, by tradition. Then man is told to consider his food, and the Day when a person will flee from his own family.

Twelve signs of the end in twelve short lines: the sun rolled up, the stars dimmed, the mountains moved, and the girl who was buried alive asked for what crime she was killed (8 to 9). Then each soul will know what it has brought. The second half swears that this is the word of a noble messenger, and that "your friend is not possessed" (22).

When the sky breaks apart and the graves are overturned, each soul will know what it sent ahead and what it left behind. "O man! What deluded you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?" (6). Over everyone are watchers who record what he does.

"Woe to the defrauders", who take full measure for themselves and give short measure to others. The record of the wicked is kept in Sijjin and that of the righteous in Illiyyun. Those who used to laugh at the believers will be laughed at in turn.

When the sky is split and the earth gives up what is in it, man will meet the Lord he has been toiling toward. One is given his book in his right hand and goes back to his people glad; another is given it behind his back and calls for death.

A curse on "the People of the Trench", who sat watching as believers were thrown into a fire for no reason but their faith in God (4 to 8). It ends by calling this "a Glorious Quran, in a Preserved Tablet" (21 to 22).
By the sky and the piercing star: every soul has a watcher over it. Let man consider what he was made from; the One who made him is able to bring him back. This is a decisive word, and no joke.

"Praise the Name of your Lord, the Most High", who creates, measures and guides. The Prophet is promised that he will be made to recite and will not forget, except what God wills (6 to 7). The one who purifies himself succeeds; and this, it says, is in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses.

On that Day some faces will be downcast, in a scorching Fire, and some joyful, in a lofty Garden. "Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?" (17). The Prophet is told: "You are only a reminder. You have no control over them" (21 to 22).

How God dealt with Aad of Iram, with Thamud and with Pharaoh. Man thinks himself honored when he prospers and insulted when he is straitened; but "you do not honor the orphan, and you do not urge the feeding of the poor" (17 to 18). It ends with the soul at peace called home: "Enter among My servants. Enter My Paradise."

Man was created into hardship, and shown the two ways. The steep way is "the freeing of a slave, or the feeding on a day of hunger an orphan near of kin, or a destitute in the dust" (13 to 16), and then to be of those who urge one another to patience and to kindness.

Seven oaths, by the sun, the moon, the day, the night, the sky, the earth and the soul, to one point: "Successful is he who purifies it; failing is he who corrupts it" (9 to 10). Thamud is the example, who killed the she-camel of God.

People's efforts differ. The one who gives and fears God will find his way made easy; the one who is stingy and thinks himself in no need will find it made hard, and his wealth will not help him when he falls.

A consolation to the Prophet: "Your Lord did not abandon you, nor did He forget." He found you an orphan and sheltered you, wandering and guided you, in need and enriched you. "Therefore, do not mistreat the orphan, nor rebuff the seeker."
"Did We not soothe your heart, and lift from you your burden?" Twice over: "With hardship comes ease." When the work is done, turn to your Lord.
By the fig and the olive, Mount Sinai and "this safe land": man was created in the best design, then brought down to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do good.

Its first five verses are, by tradition, the first words revealed to Muhammad: "Read: In the Name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot." The rest rebukes a man who forbids a servant of God to pray, and ends, "kneel down, and come near."
"We sent it down on the Night of Decree", a night "better than a thousand months", on which the angels and the Spirit descend. "Peace it is, until the rise of dawn."

The People of the Scripture and the idolaters did not divide until the clear proof came to them: a messenger from God reciting purified pages. They were commanded only to worship God with sincere devotion, to pray and to give alms (5). Those of them who disbelieve are "the worst of creatures"; those who believe and do good, "the best of creatures".

When the earth is shaken with its last quake and gives up its burdens, it will tell its news. "Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it."

An oath by horses charging at dawn, raising dust: the human being is ungrateful to his Lord, and fierce in his love of wealth. Does he not know what happens when the graves are emptied and what is in the hearts is brought out?
The Day when people will be like scattered moths and the mountains like tufted wool. The one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasant life; the one whose scales are light, a raging Fire.
"Abundance distracts you, until you visit the graveyards." Then you will see the Fire with your own eyes, and be questioned about the comforts you enjoyed.
Three verses: by Time, the human being is in loss, "except those who believe, and do good works, and encourage truth, and recommend patience".
Woe to every slanderer and backbiter who piles up wealth and counts it, thinking it will make him live forever. He will be thrown into the Crusher: the kindled Fire of God, which reaches the hearts.

"Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the People of the Elephant?" Flocks of birds pelted them with stones of baked clay. Tradition tells of an army with an elephant that marched on Mecca in the year Muhammad was born.
For the safety of Quraysh on their winter and summer journeys, "let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger, and has secured them against fear."

Who denies the religion? The one who drives away the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the poor. "Woe to those who pray" and are heedless of their prayer, who make a show, and withhold small kindnesses.
The shortest surah: "We have given you plenty. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. He who hates you is the loser."
"Say, O disbelievers: I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship." It ends, "You have your way, and I have my way."

"When there comes God's victory, and conquest, and you see the people entering God's religion in multitudes, then celebrate the praise of your Lord, and seek His forgiveness." By tradition, among the last surahs to be revealed.

A curse on Abu Lahab (an uncle of Muhammad and his opponent, by tradition) and on his wife: his wealth will not help him, and he will burn in a flaming Fire. He is the only contemporary opponent of the Prophet whom the Quran names.
Four verses that state the oneness of God: "He is God, the One. God, the Absolute. He begets not, nor was He begotten. And there is nothing comparable to Him."
A prayer for refuge with the Lord of daybreak: from the evil of what He created, of the darkness as it gathers, of those who practice sorcery, and of the envier when he envies.
A prayer for refuge with the Lord, the King, the God of mankind, from the whisperer who whispers into people's hearts, "from among jinn and among people".
